item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q024_fibronectin_fragment_selection","answer":"In SCOPe 2.08 both d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 are reference domains in family b.1.2.1, the Fibronectin type III family, within superfamily b.1.2, fold b.1 immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich, and class b all-beta proteins. The fragment annotation on d1o5dt2 is local to that domain record: d1o5dt2 is 1o5d chain T residues 107-205, in the extracellular region of human tissue factor, and SCOPe marks it `fr`, meaning that the domain is missing more than one-third of the common structure and/or sequence. d1uc6a1, 1uc6 chain A residues 6-109 from human ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha, has the same family SCCS but no corresponding fragment inconsistency in the returned annotation record.\n\nThat means d1o5dt2 should still be treated as a homologous member of b.1.2.1 for evolutionary classification, not moved to a weaker fold-only or superfamily-only relationship solely because it is partial. However, the partial record is a poor stand-alone description of the family’s full residue span: alignments using it should be interpreted as fragment-to-domain alignments with uncovered positions expected, its endpoints should not be transferred as complete fibronectin type III boundaries, and gaps caused by the missing common core should not be counted as true insertions or deletions in the intact family. For representative selection, d1uc6a1 or another complete domain is the safer representative for the common fibronectin type III topology; d1o5dt2 can document the tissue-factor subcase but should be flagged, down-weighted, or excluded when selecting a representative intended to cover full-length family diversity. The annotation also limits interpretation of apparent diversity: differences unique to d1o5dt2 may reflect truncation or unresolved/missing structural material rather than a distinct complete domain architecture, so the fragment should not by itself create a new representative cluster, imply that b.1.2.1 spans a shorter fold, or justify transferring tissue-factor-specific function to ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha.","evidence_used":["get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/current","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1uc6a1","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1uc6a1/parents","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1uc6a1/annotations","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1uc6a1/homology","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1o5dt2","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1o5dt2/parents","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1o5dt2/annotations","get_scop_domains: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sids/d1o5dt2/homology","get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/49266","get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/49266/parents","get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/49266/annotations","get_scop_node: /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/49266/homology"]}]}
